definition.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change; also called decarbonisation.

facts.text: The IPCC defines it as a human intervention to reduce emissions or enhance the sinks of greenhouse gases.
Main actions are saving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy; changing land use and removing CO2 are secondary strategies.
There are four types of measures: sustainable energy and transport, energy conservation, sustainable agriculture and green industry, and enhancing sinks and carbon removal.
2022 assessments said emissions must peak before 2025 and fall about 43% by 2030 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.
Adopted policies would still lead to about 2.7 °C of warming by 2100, well above the Paris Agreement goal.
Solar and wind can replace fossil fuels at the lowest cost of the renewable options.
Air travel and cement production are among the processes hardest to decarbonise.
Mitigation is often seen as a burden to share, but it can also be an opportunity for industrial development and exports.

definition.text: Cutting emissions by reducing demand for the goods and services that cause them, through behaviour, infrastructure and end-use technology.

facts.text: Examples include eating less meat, building good public transport and insulating houses.
Demand-side solutions could cut global greenhouse gas emissions by 40% to 70% by 2050 while improving well-being.
The richest 10% of people cause about half of all lifestyle emissions.
High-impact personal actions include flying less, avoiding petrol cars, eating mainly plants and electrifying homes.

title: Energy conservation
article: Climate change mitigation#Energy conservation and efficiency

definition.text: Reducing energy consumption by using less of an energy service, for example by driving less.

facts.text: Energy conservation sits at the top of the sustainable energy hierarchy.
Burning fossil fuels for transport and electricity is less than 50% efficient, with much heat wasted.
More efficient buildings, industry and transport could cut the world's energy needs in 2050 by one third.

definition.text: Eating fewer animal products and more plant-based food to cut the greenhouse gas emissions caused by food.

facts.text: Food is the largest share of consumption-based emissions, nearly 20% of the global carbon footprint.
Widespread vegetarian diets could cut food-related emissions by 63% by 2050.
Returning land used for animal farming to nature could sequester 100 billion tonnes of CO2 by 2100.

definition.text: Side benefits of cutting emissions beyond slowing climate change, such as cleaner air, better health, jobs and energy security; also called ancillary benefits.

facts.text: Fossil-fuel air pollution is estimated to kill over 5 million people a year as of 2019.
Replacing coal plants with renewables can more than double the jobs per megawatt of capacity in some cases.
Countries that import energy can gain independence and supply security by building renewables.
The IPCC noted in 2007 that co-benefits are often neglected and not quantified or monetised by decision-makers.
Counting co-benefits properly can change decisions about when and how much to mitigate.

definition.text: Harms and risks that some mitigation measures can cause, such as damage to biodiversity or mining pressure on conservation areas.

facts.text: Mining metals and minerals for renewable energy can threaten conservation areas.
Focusing on risks can produce deadlock, because people weigh possible losses more than benefits.

definition.text: What it costs economies to cut emissions, which depends on the baseline scenario, modelling choices, policy assumptions and timing.

facts.text: Economists estimate mitigation costs at between 1% and 2% of GDP, far less than the IMF's estimate of over $5 trillion a year in fossil fuel subsidies.
The Stern Review put the cost of inaction at least 5% of global GDP every year, up to 20% or more with wider risks, against about 2% for mitigation.
Early, well-planned action keeps costs down, and delayed global cooperation raises them.
Policymakers compare the marginal abatement costs of different measures, which differ by country, sector and time.
Uniform carbon prices bring higher costs to carbon-intensive, fossil-exporting and poorer regions.
Cost–benefit analysis may not suit mitigation as a whole but helps compare 1.5 °C and 2 °C targets.

title: Sharing the costs of emissions cuts
article: Climate change mitigation#Distributing emissions abatement costs

definition.text: The question of how responsibility for cutting emissions, and its costs, should be divided among regions, income groups and sectors.

facts.text: Proposed principles include egalitarianism, basic needs, proportionality and the polluter-pays principle.
'Equal per capita entitlements' allocate emissions either by population or by also counting historical emissions.

definition.text: Countries' announced emission targets and how much warming they would lead to if carried out.

facts.text: In November 2021 Climate Action Tracker projected 2.7 °C of warming by 2100 under current policies.
Meeting all announced targets would make warming peak at 1.9 °C and fall to 1.8 °C by 2100.
Only the EU, UK, Chile and Costa Rica had detailed official plans for their 2030 targets.

title: Coal-to-gas switching
article: Climate change mitigation#Replacing coal with natural gas

definition.text: Replacing coal with natural gas to cut emissions in the short term.

facts.text: Burning gas gives about half the emissions of coal for electricity and about two-thirds for heat.
Methane leaks during extraction and transport can cancel out the gain.
It is no path to net zero, and new gas infrastructure risks carbon lock-in and stranded assets.

title: Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks
article: Climate change mitigation#Preserving and enhancing carbon sinks

definition.text: Managing Earth's natural carbon sinks so they keep or increase their ability to take CO2 from the air and store it durably.

facts.text: Globally the two most important carbon sinks are vegetation and the ocean.
Examples are preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by reforestation.
Ecosystem restoration and less land conversion are among the tools that can cut the most emissions before 2030.
The economic potential of forest and ecosystem measures is 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq per year.
The Stern Review said in 2007 that curbing deforestation was a highly cost-effective way to cut emissions.

definition.text: The grouping of emission cuts by the part of the economy where they happen: buildings, transport, industry, and agriculture, forestry and land use.

facts.text: Buildings account for 23% of global energy-related CO2 emissions; about half their energy goes to heating space and water.
Transport causes 15% of emissions; public transport, cycling, electric vehicles and rail help cut them.
Counting direct and indirect emissions, industry is the largest emitter; electrification, green hydrogen and circular economy measures can cut them.
Agriculture and forestry cause almost 20% of emissions, and cattle produce 21% of global methane.
A modern heat pump moves about three to five times more heat energy than the electricity it uses.

definition.text: The individual, institutional and market obstacles that hold back cutting emissions.

facts.text: Finance is a major barrier for land-based options, and accounting for carbon removal is an economic barrier.
Developing countries face a shortage of capital, which rose in cost in the early 2020s.
Only 0.12% of climate research funding goes to the social science of mitigation.
